claims.text: Management is the activity of getting a business’s objectives achieved through the work of other people, and the syllabus divides that activity into four functions: planning, organising, directing and controlling.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Planning is deciding what the business is trying to achieve over a stated period and how it will get there: setting objectives, choosing between courses of action, and committing resources and a timescale to the course chosen.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Organising is arranging people, tasks, authority and resources so that the plan can be carried out, which means settling who does what, who reports to whom, what each part of the work is given, and which decisions are delegated.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Directing, which older accounts call commanding, is the day-to-day work of instructing, guiding and motivating staff so that the tasks set out in the plan are actually carried out.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Controlling has two halves: comparing what actually happened with what the plan said should happen, and acting on the difference. Measurement that nobody acts on is not control.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The four functions work as a loop rather than a sequence that ends: what controlling reveals becomes an input to the next round of planning, and a function carried out weakly undermines the ones that depend on it, so an objective not stated as a figure and a date leaves controlling with nothing definite to compare actual results against.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Fayol described the content of a manager’s job as five functions: forecasting and planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling. Coordinating is the one the four traditional functions do not name separately, and it means making the separate parts of a business act in step with each other.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Fayol’s account is prescriptive: it sets out what a manager ought to be doing, and it was drawn from his own experience of running a large mining and metals firm rather than from observation of managers at work.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mintzberg observed managers at work and described what they did as ten roles in three groups: interpersonal roles (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational roles (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson) and decisional roles (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mintzberg found managerial work to be fragmented and largely reactive - many short activities, frequent interruptions, and much of it done by talking rather than by writing or analysing - rather than the orderly sequence of functions that a list of functions suggests.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The two accounts answer different questions rather than competing: Fayol’s functions describe the purposes a manager’s work serves, while Mintzberg’s roles describe the forms that work takes while it is being done, so an hour spent settling an argument between two shifts is the disturbance-handler role and serves the purpose of directing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each account has a use and a weakness. A list of functions can be written into a job description and used to ask whether a purpose is being neglected, but it makes the job look more orderly and deliberate than a working day is. The roles describe the day accurately, but are harder to turn into a statement of what a manager should do next, because a description of what managers do is not a statement of what they ought to do.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In the syllabus phrase “the contribution of managers to business performance” the word contribution carries its everyday meaning - the part managers play in producing the result. It is not the costing term met in topic 5.4, and the formula of selling price minus variable cost does not apply to it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Managers affect business performance through five routes that can be named separately: setting direction, so that effort goes to work that serves an objective; coordinating, so that resources are not left idle waiting for each other; motivating and retaining staff; allocating scarce money, equipment and attention between competing uses; and controlling, so that a problem is found while there is still time to act on it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The part managers play shows up in measurable indicators rather than impressions: labour turnover, absenteeism, output per worker, cost per unit, the proportion of orders delivered on time, customer retention, and whether the objectives that were set were met.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Managing staff so that fewer of them leave lowers spending on recruiting and training replacements and leaves a more experienced workforce, which tends to reduce the defect rate and the time taken per unit and so lowers cost per unit; the saving is worth calculating because the cost of replacing one employee is usually larger than it looks.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How much of a business’s performance can be credited to its managers is limited by three things: external conditions the managers do not control, such as a drought, an exchange-rate movement or a new competitor; the joint nature of the output, which makes one manager’s separate share of a result hard to isolate; and the lag between a management decision and its measurable effect.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Management style is the way a manager takes decisions and deals with the people they manage - chiefly how much say those people have in a decision, and how closely their work is directed once the decision has been taken.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The four styles the syllabus names differ mainly along one dimension, how much of the decision the manager keeps: autocratic keeps the decision and issues it as an instruction, paternalistic keeps the decision but explains it and weighs what the manager judges to be good for staff, democratic shares the decision so that staff views change the outcome, and laissez-faire hands the method over entirely once the objective is agreed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A second dimension runs across the first - how much personal concern the manager shows for the individual - and it is what separates paternalistic from autocratic, since both keep the decision. The styles are points on a range rather than four separate boxes, so a manager who consults about the holiday rota and decides alone about fire procedure is matching the style to the decision rather than being inconsistent.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which style suits a situation depends on four things: how urgent the decision is, how skilled and experienced the staff are, how serious the consequences of a wrong decision would be, and what the manager believes about the people they manage.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Autocratic management is a style in which the manager takes decisions alone and passes them down as instructions, with little or no consultation and with communication running mostly one way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Three conditions favour an autocratic style: a decision that has to be taken faster than a discussion can be held, because one person deciding is quicker than a group agreeing; staff who are new or unskilled and so have little to add to the decision and need clear instruction; and a decision whose consequences are severe, such as handling chemicals or working at height, where a manager may reasonably refuse to put the method to a vote.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An autocratic style costs a business in four traceable ways: the knowledge of the people doing the job never enters the decision; being told rather than asked tends to lower the sense of being valued, so motivation may fall and absenteeism and labour turnover may rise, which raises spending on recruiting and training; the manager becomes a bottleneck, because nothing needing a decision moves while they are away; and staff who do not take decisions do not learn to take them, so the business has fewer people ready to promote.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Democratic management is a style in which the manager consults the people affected and lets their views influence the decision, with communication running both ways. In most businesses the manager still takes the decision and still answers for it; what makes the style democratic is that staff views genuinely change the outcome.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A democratic style works through two mechanisms. Information: staff who do the job hold knowledge the manager does not, so on questions about how work is done, consulting them tends to produce a better decision. Commitment: people carry out a decision they helped shape with more willingness than one handed to them, so it is implemented as intended rather than followed to the letter and no further. Consulting staff also develops them, which gives the business people who can be promoted.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A democratic style costs a business in three ways: it is slow, so a decision needed this afternoon cannot wait for a meeting; it depends on staff knowing enough about the question, since consulting people who do not may produce a worse decision than the manager would have taken alone; and it raises an expectation, so staff consulted on most decisions may resent one taken without them even where urgency made consultation impractical.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Laissez-faire management is a style in which the manager agrees the objective and then leaves staff to decide for themselves how to achieve it, intervening little. It is a deliberate handing over of the method by a manager who has set an objective, agreed a deadline and provided resources; a manager who has done none of those is absent rather than laissez-faire.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A laissez-faire style suits skilled, self-motivated specialists whose work a manager could not direct in detail anyway - a research chemist, an architect, a software developer, a designer - because given room such staff may try approaches the manager would not have thought of, and because being trusted with the method tends to make people take ownership of the result.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A laissez-faire style costs a business in three ways: without agreed objectives and check-points, work can drift for months before anyone notices and the deadline may by then be unrecoverable; coordination suffers, because people choosing their own methods separately may make choices that do not fit together; and staff who want guidance, such as anyone new to the task, can be left floundering.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Paternalistic management is a style in which the manager takes the decision but explains the reasoning behind it and takes the welfare and interests of staff into account in making it, acting, as the word suggests, like a parent deciding for a family. Consultation may happen, but the decision is not transferred.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A paternalistic style works through two mechanisms: explaining a decision rather than announcing it makes it easier to carry out, because staff who understand the reason can apply it to cases the instruction did not cover; and visible concern for welfare tends to build loyalty, so staff stay longer and experience is kept in the business. It suits a workforce that is young or inexperienced and needs direction but responds badly to being ordered.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A paternalistic style costs a business in three ways: staff still have no real say, which skilled and experienced people may find harder to accept than plain autocracy because the style invites them to feel consulted while leaving the decision where it was; it depends on the manager judging correctly what is good for staff, and a benefit nobody wanted is still money spent; and staff accustomed to having decisions made in their interest may not develop the habit of taking decisions themselves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Paternalistic differs from autocratic in two things and not in who decides, since both keep the decision: the paternalistic manager explains the reason, and weighs what is good for staff as part of making the decision. It differs from democratic not in whether a conversation happens but in whether staff views change the outcome: democratic gives staff influence over the decision, paternalistic gives them consideration without influence.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: McGregor’s Theory X is a set of assumptions a manager may hold about people: that the average person dislikes work and avoids it where possible, must therefore be directed, closely supervised and pushed by the threat of penalty, prefers to be told what to do, avoids responsibility, has little ambition, and wants security above everything else.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: McGregor’s Theory Y is the opposing set of assumptions: that effort at work is as natural as rest or play, that people will direct and control themselves in pursuit of objectives they are committed to, that commitment follows from the satisfaction of achieving something, that under the right conditions people seek responsibility rather than avoid it, and that imagination and ingenuity are widely spread in a workforce and largely under-used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Theory X and Theory Y are two sets of assumptions a manager holds about people, not two types of worker. McGregor’s argument is that a manager acts on a theory about people whether or not the manager has ever stated it, and that the theory shapes how the manager manages.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The assumptions tend to confirm themselves. A manager holding Theory X assumptions supervises closely and leaves no discretion, so staff have no opportunity to show initiative and no reward for offering an idea, and the minimum effort the manager then observes is read as proof that the assumptions were right - although the behaviour was produced by the management rather than discovered by it. The loop runs the other way for Theory Y, and in both directions it is a tendency rather than a certainty, since a decision delegated to someone without the knowledge to take it is lost control rather than Theory Y.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Theory X assumptions tend to produce autocratic practice, and can equally produce paternalistic practice where the manager believes staff must be looked after rather than driven; Theory Y assumptions tend to produce democratic practice, and laissez-faire practice where staff are skilled enough for it. The link is a tendency rather than a definition, because the situation intervenes: a manager with Theory Y assumptions running an evacuation gives orders without consulting.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Two limitations bound the framework. It describes assumptions rather than evidence, so it does not establish what people are actually like, and a manager may hold Theory Y assumptions about a workforce they do not fit. And Theory Y is not automatically the better set to hold: applying it where staff are inexperienced, the work is safety-critical or the deadline is immediate may produce worse results than direction would, so which set serves a business better depends on the work and on the people doing it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
